**Hydrogen – Key Physical, Chemical, and Isotopic Properties**

| Category | Property | Value / Description |
|----------|----------|---------------------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ |
| | Ionization energy (first) | 13.598 eV (1312 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV (–72.8 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 |
| | Atomic radius | ~31 pm (covalent) |
| | Van der Waals radius | ~120 pm |
| | Density (STP) | 0.0899 g L⁻¹ |
| | Molar volume (STP) | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) |
| | Heat capacity (gas, 298 K) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Thermal conductivity (298 K) | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Specific heat (liquid, 20 K) | 14.3 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹ |
| | Speed of sound (gas, 298 K) | 1270 m s⁻¹ |
| | Refractive index (gas, 589 nm) | 1.000132 |
| | Dielectric constant (gas) | 1.000132 |
| | Magnetic susceptibility (gas) | –2.5 × 10⁻⁶ cm³ mol⁻¹ |
| **Chemical Properties** | State at STP | Colorless, odorless, tasteless gas |
| | Diatomic molecule | H₂ |
| | Bond dissociation energy (H–H) | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ |
| | Oxidation states | +1 (proton), –1 (hydride) |
| | Acidic behavior | Acts as a proton donor (H⁺) in aqueous solution |
| | Basic behavior | Acts as a hydride donor (H⁻) in organometallic chemistry |
| | Combustion reaction | 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O (exothermic, ΔH ≈ –286 kJ mol⁻¹) |
| | Redox potential (H⁺/H₂) | 0 V vs SHE (standard hydrogen electrode) |
| | Solubility in water | ~1.6 g L⁻¹ at 25 °C (≈0.02 mol L⁻¹) |
| | Solubility in organic solvents | Very low in non‑polar solvents; higher in polar aprotic solvents |
| | Hydrogen bonding | H₂ does not form H‑bonds; H⁺ (proton) participates in H‑bonding in acids |
| | Spectroscopic signatures | Rotational spectrum (ν₀ ≈ 2 cm⁻¹), vibrational frequency (ν ≈ 4401 cm⁻¹) |
| | Isotopic substitution effects | Deuterium and tritium shift vibrational frequencies by ≈√(m_H/m_D) |
| **Isotopes** | Protium (¹H) | Stable, most abundant (≈99.98 %) |
| | Deuterium (²H, D) | Stable, 1.1 % natural abundance |
| | Tritium (³H, T) | Radioactive (half‑life 12.32 y), used in nuclear fusion research |
| | Isotopic mass differences | ¹H: 1.007825 u; ²H: 2.014102 u; ³H: 3.016049 u |
| | Isotopic effects on physical properties | Deuterium has higher boiling/melting points, lower vapor pressure, and slower diffusion |
| **Applications & Roles** | Energy carrier | Hydrogen fuel cells, rocket propellant |
| | Chemical feedstock | Production of ammonia (NH₃), methanol (CH₃OH), and other hydrogenated compounds |
| | Metallurgy | Hydrogen embrittlement of metals; used in hydrogen annealing |
| | Analytical chemistry | Used as a standard in NMR (¹H), mass spectrometry (H₂⁺), and as a carrier gas in chromatography |
| | Astrophysics & cosmology | Traces of primordial nucleosynthesis; H I 21‑cm line in radio astronomy |
| | Fusion research | Deuterium–tritium fusion (D–T) reaction in tokamaks and inertial confinement |
| | Biological systems | Proton transfer in enzymes, photosynthesis, and cellular respiration |
| **Safety & Handling** | Flammability range (air) | 4 %–75 % (by volume) |
| | Explosion limits | Lower explosive limit (LEL) ≈ 4 %; upper explosive limit (UEL) ≈ 75 % |
| | Ignition energy | ≈0.02 mJ (very low) |
| | Toxicity | Non‑toxic; however, high concentrations can displace oxygen leading to asphyxiation |
| | Storage | Requires high‑pressure cylinders (up to 700 bar) or cryogenic tanks (liquid H₂) |
| | Environmental impact | Low; combustion produces only water vapor |

---

### Quick Takeaways

- **Hydrogen is the simplest element**: one proton, one electron, and no neutrons in its most common isotope (protium).
- **It exists as a diatomic gas (H₂)** under normal conditions, with a very weak H–H bond.
- **Physical properties**: extremely light, low density, low boiling/melting points, and high speed of sound.
- **Chemical versatility**: acts as both a proton donor (acidic) and a hydride donor (basic) depending on context.
- **Isotopic diversity**: stable protium and deuterium, radioactive tritium—each with distinct physical and chemical behaviors.
- **Industrial importance**: key feedstock for ammonia, methanol, and other chemicals; central to hydrogen fuel cells and fusion research.
- **Safety considerations**: highly flammable, low ignition energy, and potential asphyxiation hazard at high concentrations.

Feel free to ask if you’d like deeper details on any specific property or application!
